drug_class: FGF23 Blocker (Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 Inhibitor) / Monoclonal Antibody
purpose: Burosumab-Twza is used to treat a rare condition called X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH), which causes low phosphate levels in the blood and leads to weak, soft bones. It is also used for a related condition called tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO). This medicine helps your body keep enough phosphate so your bones can grow and stay strong.
how_it_works: In people with XLH or TIO, a protein called FGF23 is overactive and causes the kidneys to flush out too much phosphate through urine. Burosumab-Twza is a special antibody that blocks FGF23, like putting a stop sign on it. This allows your kidneys to hold onto phosphate, raising the levels in your blood so your bones and body can work the way they should.
common_side_effects: Injection site reactions such as redness, swelling, or itching where the shot was given. You may also notice headaches, fever, rash, pain in your arms or legs, tooth or dental problems, back pain, and nausea. In children, vitamin D levels and bone pain may change as treatment begins.
warnings: Do not use this medicine if your phosphate levels are already normal or high, as it could raise phosphate too much and cause calcification (hardening) in your kidneys or other tissues. Tell your doctor right away if you have kidney problems. Your doctor will monitor your phosphate, vitamin D, and kidney function regularly. Let your doctor know all medications you take, especially phosphate supplements or active vitamin D, as these may need to be stopped before starting this medicine.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous shot), usually every 2 weeks for children and every 4 weeks for adults. The exact dose depends on your weight and age, and your doctor will calculate the right amount for you. It is typically given in a clinic or doctor's office, though some patients may learn to give it at home.
